Title: Lifecycle and invocation metadata is recorded
What we implement: Nothing. Reports NOT_APPLICABLE, with two observations recorded as evidence: whether each result names its server in _meta, and whether the server advertises the deprecated logging capability.
Why: The audit samples the deployment's own log. The server-identity field has a wire source, but only one of several: a logger can take the identity from its own configuration, so its absence on the wire is not a failure of this recommendation.
Not covered: The whole recommendation. The timestamp, correlation identifier, event-type inventory and central shipping are all log-side. The negotiated revision is recorded alongside, because reporting identity per result is a 2026-07-28 recommendation the protocol marks optional.

Title: Non-null JSON-RPC request IDs are enforced and included in audit logs
What we implement: That a request whose JSON-RPC id is null is refused rather than accepted.
Why: The protocol states the rule directly and a refusal is visible to any client. A server that accepts a null id cannot pair a response to its request.
How: One otherwise-conformant tools/list carrying a null id, sent authenticated so it reaches id validation instead of stopping at a 401. A success result or a 2xx with no body is an acceptance and fails, and the evidence names which. A rejection passes even with a different status or code, both named. A non-2xx with no JSON-RPC error object is ERROR, because a gateway produces exactly that.
Not covered: Whether the request id reaches the audit log. Also the outstanding-id collision rule: discrete HTTP requests cannot hold one in flight while a second reuses its id, and the audit does not test it either. One further limit is on our side rather than the server's: the access token is read once when the session starts, and a refresh during the run retires it. The request then draws 401 and the check reports UNKNOWN rather than a verdict, which is what happened on one target.

Title: Audit records carry accurate, monotonic timestamps
Why: The requirement is stated against values recorded in the log rather than against any host time service, and MCP carries no timestamp on the wire, so there is nothing to compare.

Title: Alerts are generated on audience and issuer validation failures
What we implement: That the server refuses a token the authorization server minted for a different resource.
Why: This is enforcement rather than self-description, so it is stronger evidence than reading the audience of our own token. The server either refuses a foreign-audience token or it does not.
How: Reuses the token check 3.3.1b already obtained, so no second refresh grant is spent. A control request with the valid token must succeed first, otherwise a 401 may only mean the endpoint refuses everything. Registered last, because obtaining that token spends a refresh grant.
Not covered: The structured event, the alerting rule and the routing to an operator, which are the recommendation's actual subject. Client-side issuer validation binds the client, which is this probe. Reports UNKNOWN where the authorization server refuses to mint the token, which is the conforming answer and the common case.

Title: notifications/cancelled and notifications/progress are monitored for behavioral anomalies
What we implement: That every notification names the server that sent it, and that every progress notification echoes a progressToken this run sent.
Why: Both are preconditions the operator's monitoring rests on. A notification with no identity cannot be attributed, and a progress notification whose token matches nothing cannot be correlated. The benchmark names a notification lacking server identity as a failure in its own words.
How: Reads the notifications the run already receives. The progressToken rides on a tool call another check already makes, so no invocation is added, and the comparison is against every token sent because a notification for another call is correct.
Not covered: The per-server baselines and the anomaly rules. Cancellation by notification is the stdio path, and on Streamable HTTP a cancellation is a closed response stream, observable only at the server or its gateway. Task lifecycle keyed by taskId is not probed. Three absences are reported distinctly: no stream opened, nothing arrived, or nothing was a progress notification.
